tables.how: The program descriptions that each organization files with the IRS (Form 990, Part III, line 4, and the notes on it in Schedule O) were read by rule in every full return on file, the latest version of each. A figure is a number followed by a unit of service, such as people, families, youth, meals or visits. A sentence counts as repeated when the same sentence with the same figure, capital letters aside, is in the returns of three or more tax years, speaks of serving, providing or the like, has a figure of 100 or more and is not worded as a capacity, a goal or a running total. Where an organization repeats several, the one in the most returns is taken, then the largest figure. That finds 44 organizations. The case counts the 33 of them that received $250,000 or more from the City in fiscal 2026 and whose figure does not count housing units, apartments or beds. Every full return on file for each of the 33 is listed, for tax years ending 2020 to 2025: 165 returns, 122 of them with the identical sentence (19 organizations in 3 returns, 5 organizations in 4 returns, 9 organizations in 5 returns). 9 organizations carry it in every return on file; in 15 the latest return on file no longer does; in 1 the returns that carry it are not consecutive years. 1 of the 33 sentences names a year or a fiscal year. The 4 organizations in the case's numbered points come first, in the order of the points; the rest follow by their City payments in fiscal 2026, largest first. An organization is tied to its returns by its employer identification number, so the name on a return can differ from the name on the City's payments; both are shown. A sentence of more than 25 words is cut to the 25 words around the figure, with … where words are left out; sentences are compared on their first 300 characters. The City payments are those of all departments in the fiscal year with the same number as the year in which the tax year ends, in each of the Controller's two tables.
tables.limits: A repeated sentence does not show that the work was not done or that fewer people were served. Some figures describe a fixed capacity or a standing fact about the organization and would be the same every year. Tax preparers often carry last year's text forward while program staff keep accurate counts elsewhere, and what an organization reports to its City funders is separate from its tax return and is not in these records. The reading is by rule: a sentence that changed by a word or a digit is not matched, so a No can mean a new count, a reworded sentence or a dropped one, and the linked return shows which. For an organization whose tax year is the calendar year, the City's fiscal year of the same number overlaps it by six months only. The payments are every City payment to the organization, not the cost of the program the sentence describes. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.

tables.how: The case's $168.4 million is the nonprofit-spending table for fiscal 2026: the 33 organizations' rows for that year add to $168,434,190 (the case adds each organization's total after rounding it to the dollar, $168,434,192). The table of every payment has $206,856,892 for the same organizations and year. The four organizations in the case's numbered points received Eviction Defense Collaborative Inc $17,408,300; Swords To Plowshares-Veterans Rights Org $5,188,218; Mission Cultural Center For Latino Arts $701,466; Cross Cultural Family Center $276,703 in fiscal 2026. Each organization's payments in the two tables the Controller publishes, as retrieved on 12 November 2026: Citywide Nonprofit Spending, which by its own description keeps contracted services only, and Vendor Payments (Vouchers), the table of every payment. The fiscal year is the one printed on the payment. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus the renames and spellings that a shared contract number confirms.
tables.limits: The payments are for everything the City bought from each organization, of which the program described in the repeated sentence may be a small part or no part. A large payment beside a repeated sentence is not a finding about the payment. A payment is money the City sent, not money the organization kept or spent on itself: subsidies, rent aid and grants that an organization pays on to others are in these figures. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment or a contract; neither is wrong for that reason. The year printed on a payment can be later than the year the payment was issued. A payee the City spells in a way that no contract number ties to the organization is not counted.

tables.how: The program descriptions that each organization files with the IRS (Form 990, Part III, line 4, and the notes on it in Schedule O) were read by rule in every full return on file, the latest version of each. A figure is a number followed by a unit of service, such as people, families, youth, meals or visits. A sentence counts as repeated when the same sentence with the same figure, capital letters aside, is in the returns of three or more tax years, speaks of serving, providing or the like, has a figure of 100 or more and is not worded as a capacity, a goal or a running total. Where an organization repeats several, the one in the most returns is taken, then the largest figure. The first list gives one sentence for each organization. 12 of the 33 repeat others as well, 23 sentences in all; each is listed here once for every return that carries it, with its figure and the unit word and without the sentence, which the linked return shows.
tables.limits: A repeated sentence does not show that the work was not done or that fewer people were served. Some figures describe a fixed capacity or a standing fact about the organization and would be the same every year. Tax preparers often carry last year's text forward while program staff keep accurate counts elsewhere, and what an organization reports to its City funders is separate from its tax return and is not in these records. The reading is by rule: a sentence that changed by a word or a digit is not matched, so a No can mean a new count, a reworded sentence or a dropped one, and the linked return shows which. Two of an organization's repeated sentences can describe the same program in different words. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.
